questions.title: Previously treated extrahepatic disease
questions.question: May a patient whose extrahepatic HCC (including proven lymph-node metastasis) was treated and has responded completely ever enter a transplant route, or does this history close transplantation?
questions.position: Keep closed. A history of extrahepatic metastasis or proven nodal metastasis excludes the standard OPTN route and every HCC high-risk cohort, even after resection, ablation, radiotherapy or a complete response to immunotherapy. Record durable complete responders in a prospective registry; this edition offers no transplant route.
rules: “No extrahepatic disease” in HCC-B1 and HCC-B2 means no current or previous extrahepatic metastasis. Resection, ablation, radiotherapy or a complete radiological response does not clear this history.

Count proven lymph-node metastasis, including hilar or hepatoduodenal nodes, as extrahepatic disease. Enlarged hilar nodes without proof are HOLD for characterization. A lesion later proven benign is not prior extrahepatic disease; record how it was resolved.

Registry, not listing: enter durable complete responders with dated imaging, AFP and treatment history. Starting points for any future study (not active): ≥12 months without evidence of disease off systemic therapy; PET or tissue confirmation that every extrahepatic site is cleared; current whole-body staging including bone; an immunotherapy washout of ≥90 days and the HCC-B3 safety review.
Do not combine with the expanded-burden (HCC-B1) or portal-vein invasion (HCC-B2) cohorts.
questions.why: The guidelines describe current extrahepatic disease only. Excluding previously treated disease is this program’s inference, stated as such: no series reports outcomes of transplantation after treated extrahepatic HCC (cohorts that contain such recipients exclude them or do not report them separately), nodal disease at transplantation strongly predicts recurrence, and a complete response to immunotherapy is not cure.

evidence.selection: Every extrahepatic-disease statement is in the present tense (downstaging, immunotherapy for downstaging, LDLT with vascular invasion). Lymph nodes are not mentioned.
evidence.results: No recommendation on how long to observe after a response to immunotherapy; the only long interval specified is ≥12 months after downstaging of Vp1–2 invasion.
evidence.limits: Consensus; silent on previously treated extrahepatic disease and on nodes.
evidence.locator: Liver Cancer 2026; Table 1, Working Groups B–C.

evidence.selection: Table 4 lists “lymph node involvement by tumor or extrahepatic spread of tumor” as downstaging failure and exclusion from transplantation.
evidence.results: Recommends stopping immune checkpoint inhibitors at least 3 months before transplantation.
evidence.limits: No section addresses transplantation or resection after treated extrahepatic disease.
evidence.locator: Hepatology 2023; Table 4 and transplant section (relevant sections read).

evidence.design_population: Single case: nodal, lung, mediastinal and bone metastases treated with nivolumab.
evidence.selection: Only reported transplant after distant HCC.
evidence.results: Best response to nivolumab was partial (RECIST 1.1); the authors’ later “complete response” is not documented by RECIST, PET or biopsy; bone lesions did not clearly regress; liver disease recurred off nivolumab and was ablated; transplanted about 15 months after the last dose; cancer-free 1 year later.
evidence.limits: Extrahepatic clearance never confirmed by biopsy or PET; no nodes examined in the explant; one case with 1-year follow-up.

evidence.design_population: Four-centre cohort of 160 complete responders to immunotherapy-based therapy.
evidence.selection: 58 (36%) had extrahepatic metastases when immunotherapy started.
evidence.results: Prior extrahepatic metastasis doubled recurrence risk after complete response (adjusted HR 2.00, 95% CI 1.43–6.38); 5-year recurrence-free survival 18% in the whole cohort.
evidence.limits: Retrospective; conversion subgroup of 11 not split by extrahepatic status; internal numeric inconsistencies.

evidence.design_population: Eight-centre matched cohort, 416 recipients beyond Milan.
evidence.selection: Extrahepatic metastasis was an exclusion (9 transplanted patients left out).
evidence.results: Immunotherapy-based downstaging associated with better survival (HR 0.63); acute rejection 16.3% vs 8.2%, clustered with washout ≤90 days.
evidence.limits: Not evidence for treated extrahepatic disease; transplanted-only cohort.

evidence.design_population: Meta-analysis of transplant series: five on recurrence and five more on survival.
evidence.selection: Hilar nodes examined at transplantation.
evidence.results: Tumor-positive nodes associated with recurrence (common odds ratio 10.44, 95% CI 3.43–38.59).
evidence.limits: Small, older series; nodes mostly found at transplantation.

evidence.design_population: European registry, 105 transplants for HCC in non-cirrhotic liver.
evidence.selection: Nodal status recorded.
evidence.results: Lymph-node involvement associated with death (HR 2.60, 95% CI 1.28–5.28).
evidence.limits: Non-cirrhotic HCC only; timing of nodal disease not stated.

evidence.design_population: US national cancer database, 4,329 patients on first-line immunotherapy.
evidence.selection: Only 15 patients with distant and 10 with nodal metastasis received any curative treatment afterwards; modality not reported.
evidence.results: Curative treatment after immunotherapy associated with longer survival (propensity-matched HR 0.22 in the main text).
evidence.limits: Immortal-time and indication bias; no response or recurrence data; cannot inform transplantation after treated extrahepatic disease.

questions.counter: Durable complete responses to immunotherapy now occur, and the single case shows transplantation is feasible. ILTS–ILCA states there is not enough evidence on whether complete responders still need transplantation or how long to observe them, so a permanent bar is a policy choice rather than a proven boundary.
questions.certainty: Very low for transplantation after treated or completely responded extrahepatic HCC (one case). Moderate that current nodal or extrahepatic disease predicts poor post-transplant outcome.
questions.change: A prospective series with ≥3-year post-transplant recurrence-free survival in patients whose extrahepatic disease was cleared and confirmed by PET or pathology, or an explicit ILTS/OPTN statement on previously treated disease.

questions.title: Liver treatment after extrahepatic disease responds
questions.question: After extrahepatic HCC responds to systemic therapy or is treated locally, when should resection or ablation of the liver tumor be offered?
questions.position: Offer curative-intent liver resection or ablation, with treatment of every residual extrahepatic site, only to selected patients after MDT review, and present it as life-prolonging multimodal therapy, not cure. Use the JLCA definition of localized extrahepatic spread; all other extrahepatic disease stays systemic-therapy-led. This roadmap position does not open transplantation (HCC-B5).
rules: Localized extrahepatic spread (JLCA 2023, BR1): a solitary node at station 3, 8 or 12; localized peritoneal disease (P1); a unilateral adrenal metastasis; or a few lung metastases. All other extrahepatic disease is BR2: benefit of surgery uncertain.

Before surgery: response or stable disease of every extrahepatic site on serial imaging, no new lesions, current whole-body staging, every intrahepatic and extrahepatic site treatable (resection, ablation or stereotactic radiotherapy), adequate liver reserve, ECOG 0–1. No guideline sets the interval; the MDT records the interval it uses.

AASLD 2023 does not support systemic therapy before resection outside trials. Record the decision as an MDT exception or enroll in a study or registry; plan continued systemic therapy and surveillance.

Counsel that recurrence is the rule: after stereotactic radiotherapy to oligometastases, 2-year progression-free survival was 0%; after borderline-resectable surgery, 3-year recurrence-free survival was 19.7%.
questions.why: National and multicentre cohorts associate surgery after response with longer survival, but every comparison is biased toward the operated patients. JLCA gives the only explicit definition of the limited extrahepatic disease for which surgery may help.

evidence.design_population: Japanese expert consensus on oncological resectability (17 panelists).
evidence.selection: Statement 9 (15/17): extrahepatic spread is basically BR2; localized spread could be BR1 (solitary node at station 3, 8 or 12; P1 peritoneum; unilateral adrenal; few lung metastases).
evidence.results: Cites 5-year survival of 29.5% after resection of node-positive HCC and 27–66% after lung metastasectomy.
evidence.limits: Surgeon-only panel; a classification, not a treatment recommendation; permissive (“could be”); no response or interval criteria.

evidence.design_population: 15-centre cohort, 150 patients with extrahepatic metastases whose intrahepatic tumor reached partial or complete response (mRECIST).
evidence.selection: Only 8 of 26 operated patients had their metastases removed; 85% had partial (not complete) response of extrahepatic disease.
evidence.results: Median survival 16.5 vs 11.3 months from response (surgery vs none); progression-free survival not different.
evidence.limits: Immortal-time bias; operated patients more often oligometastatic; counts inconsistent.

evidence.design_population: US national cancer database, 4,329 patients on first-line immunotherapy.
evidence.selection: 138 (3.2%) had curative treatment afterwards, including 15 with distant and 10 with nodal metastasis.
evidence.results: Propensity-matched HR 0.22 (0.14–0.33) for death with curative treatment.
evidence.limits: Immortal-time bias; curative intent uncertain; modality not separated for the 15 distant and 10 nodal patients.

evidence.selection: 112 with pathologically proven nodal metastasis.
evidence.results: 3-year survival 38.9% (nodal) vs 27.2% (distant stage IVB).

evidence.design_population: Comparison of 64 patients with extrahepatic recurrence and controlled liver disease.
evidence.selection: Nodes, adrenal, peritoneum, lung or brain; resectable.
evidence.results: 5-year survival 60.5% with resection vs 9.1% without.

evidence.design_population: Phase II trial, 40 patients with controlled HCC and 1–5 metastases.
evidence.selection: Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy to all metastases.
evidence.results: 2-year survival 80%; 2-year progression-free survival 0%.

evidence.design_population: Weighted comparison, 209 patients with lung oligometastases.
evidence.selection: Metastasectomy vs stereotactic radiotherapy.
evidence.results: 2-year local control 98.2% vs 97.0% (unweighted); weighted 2-year progression-free survival 23.0% vs 24.7%.
evidence.locator: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2024 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: BR1 as defined by the 2023 consensus, which includes localized extrahepatic spread; the number with extrahepatic spread is not given in the abstract.
evidence.results: 5-year disease-specific survival 40.8%; 3-year recurrence-free survival 19.7%.
evidence.limits: No extrahepatic subgroup in the abstract.
evidence.locator: J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2025 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: No section on surgery after treated extrahepatic disease.
evidence.results: Does not recommend systemic therapy before resection outside trials.

questions.counter: All cohorts select fit patients with few lesions; benefit may reflect biology rather than surgery. AASLD does not support preoperative systemic therapy outside trials.
questions.certainty: Low for longer survival after resection of limited, responded extrahepatic disease; very low for cure.
questions.change: Prospective or randomized data on surgery after response in oligometastatic HCC.

questions.title: Surgery or transplantation after nodal or extrahepatic disease
questions.question: When combined HCC–cholangiocarcinoma has nodal or extrahepatic disease that responds, is resection or transplantation reasonable?
questions.position: Resection with regional lymphadenectomy remains the curative option for organ-confined disease. After a response of regional nodal disease, decide case by case using the iCCA rules (iCCA-R1); distant extrahepatic disease stays systemic-therapy-led. Transplantation is closed after any nodal or extrahepatic disease, as in iCCA-B4.
rules: Regional nodal disease that responds: MDT case-by-case resection with lymphadenectomy; confirm response by restaging and tissue where feasible.
Distant extrahepatic disease: systemic therapy; no conversion pathway (no published data).
Transplantation: previous nodal or extrahepatic disease excludes transplantation, as for iCCA (iCCA-B4).
questions.why: In resected cHCC–CCA, nodal metastasis and local extrahepatic invasion carry large hazard ratios, and no study reports surgery after extrahepatic response. After transplantation, recurrence is frequent and mostly extrahepatic.

evidence.design_population: Single-centre cohort, 55 resections; distant metastasis excluded.
evidence.selection: Nodal metastasis in 11 (20%).
evidence.results: Nodal metastasis: survival HR 6.95 (2.15–22.44); local extrahepatic invasion HR 4.91; 5-year survival 16.4% overall.
evidence.limits: Small; survival by nodal status shown only as curves and hazard ratios, without numeric rates.

evidence.design_population: Nine-centre cohort, 111 transplant recipients with cHCC–CC.
evidence.selection: Diagnosis on explant; nodal metastasis in 3.
evidence.results: Recurrence 44.1% vs 19.1% in HCC; first recurrence extrahepatic-only in 37 of 49.
evidence.locator: World J Gastrointest Surg 2023; Results, Table 4.

evidence.selection: Nodal and extrahepatic status not reported.
evidence.results: Beyond UCSF, 5-year survival 15.8%; within Milan, transplant survival similar to HCC.
evidence.limits: Diagnosis on final pathology; only 5.3% recognized as cHCC–CCA before surgery.

evidence.selection: No tumor-level variables.
evidence.results: Lowest 15-year survival among primary liver cancers (graft-loss HR 1.79; death HR 1.67).

questions.counter: No direct study; regional nodal disease does not by itself prove futility, and nodal metastasis predicts death and recurrence (Jiang HR 6.95; Kim, 3 node-positive recipients), but no absolute survival rates by nodal status are reported.
questions.change: Any series of resection after response of nodal disease in cHCC–CCA.

questions.title: Previously treated nodal or extrahepatic disease
questions.question: Should a patient whose iCCA nodal or extrahepatic disease has responded or been resected ever be considered for transplantation?
questions.position: Keep closed. Proven nodal metastasis or extrahepatic disease, current or previously treated (including resected), excludes the small-cirrhotic route and the advanced-iCCA study. Confirm node-negative status with tissue before listing, and characterize every indeterminate extrahepatic lesion. Applies also to mixed HCC–iCCA.
rules: Previously proven malignant nodes, even after radiological or pathological response, and any previous distant metastasis (peritoneum, lung, bone, distant nodes) are outside the initial iCCA routes. Resection of an extrahepatic site does not clear this history.
Suspicious or indeterminate nodes are HOLD until resolved with tissue; an imaging response is not nodal clearance.

Advanced-iCCA study: before listing, sample stations 8 and 12 surgically, plus any suspicious node (EUS-FNA or surgical). For living donation, complete this before listing, not only at the combined donor–recipient laparotomy. A positive result ends the route.
Indeterminate extrahepatic lesions (subcentimetre lung nodules, bone lesions) need biopsy or interval imaging; “stable on chemotherapy” is not clearance.
Previously node-positive disease that has cleared is a separate future research question; do not combine it with multifocal, G3 or living-donor expansions.
questions.why: Published iCCA transplant protocols exclude proven nodal and extrahepatic disease (one pilot, Wong 2019, admitted regional lymphadenopathy), and the Milan protocol excludes even resected extrahepatic spread. In the published series, early recurrences came from nodal disease missed by imaging, from indeterminate lesions accepted as stable, or from positive margins and perihilar-fat invasion.

evidence.selection: Excluded extrahepatic metastases and lymph-node involvement; suspicious regional nodes biopsied by EUS.
evidence.results: One recipient with unbiopsied, PET-negative periportal nodes that regressed (node-negative on explant) recurred in the peritoneum at 9.7 months, attributed by the authors to perihilar-fat invasion with a positive margin; in 2 of 6, “stable” extrahepatic lesions proved metastatic after transplant.

evidence.selection: Nodal or distant metastasis defined as extrahepatic disease and excluded; delisted on extrahepatic progression.
evidence.results: Survival from listing 100/71/57% at 1/3/5 years (all listed: 90/61/49%); one explant had metastatic carcinoma in 4 of 7 hilar nodes; two early recurrences arose from indeterminate pre-transplant lesions.

evidence.selection: Excludes “prior resected extrahepatic tumor spread”; surgical sampling of stations 8 and 12 before listing.
evidence.results: Positive nodes in 2 of 6 explored, missed by imaging and PET; all 4 transplanted patients disease-free at 8–73 months.
evidence.limits: Small; abstract and Results drop-out counts differ.

evidence.design_population: UPMC living-donor series, 7 recipients (co-authored by Hao Liu).
evidence.selection: Liver-confined disease; nodes biopsied at the combined laparotomy.
evidence.results: 2 of 6 explants with viable tumor were node-positive although the protocol included nodal biopsy at the same laparotomy; one died at about 7 months; a sub-PET-threshold lung nodule became a metastasis.

evidence.selection: Explant nodal status.
evidence.results: Node positivity predicted recurrence (HR 3.27, 1.32–8.10) but not overall survival (p=0.14); in the intentional pCCA/iCCA subset (n=53) the recurrence HR was 2.48 and not significant (p=0.17).
evidence.limits: Mixed subtypes; nodes found on explant, not before.

evidence.selection: Transplant for iCCA only without extrahepatic metastasis (cirrhotic ≤3 cm) or for liver-confined disease within protocols.
evidence.results: No outcome data.

evidence.selection: Nodal invasion recorded.
evidence.results: Nodal invasion an independent predictor of death.

questions.counter: One pilot admitted regional lymphadenopathy in mixed hilar and intrahepatic tumors (5 of 18 transplanted, one nodal recurrence); whether the nodes were proven malignant is not reported in the abstract, and it cannot establish a cleared-node pathway.
questions.certainty: Low that liver-confined disease after sustained response selects better recipients; very low for transplantation after previously malignant nodes; none for previously treated distant disease.
questions.change: A protocol series with tissue-proven nodal clearance before listing and ≥3-year outcomes.

questions.title: Surgery after nodal or extrahepatic disease responds
questions.question: When regional nodes or distant metastases of iCCA respond to chemotherapy, is conversion resection reasonable?
questions.position: Regional nodal disease (hepatoduodenal and common hepatic artery area) that responds may proceed to conversion resection with lymphadenectomy after MDT review. Nodes beyond the regional basin and distant metastases stay systemic-therapy-led; conversion surgery only exceptionally, on very low-certainty evidence, inside a registry or study.
rules: Regional nodes: restage after response; sample suspicious residual nodes where feasible, because residual nodal disease in the specimen is strongly adverse.

Distant disease (non-regional nodes, liver-only oligometastases, limited peritoneal or lung): only after durable response on serial imaging, negative whole-body restaging, staging laparoscopy with nodal sampling, and complete resectability of every site.

Counsel: recurrence 35% across pooled conversion series and 70% (14 of 20) in one single-centre series; major complications 50–61% and postoperative mortality 0–9% in individual series (90-day mortality 4.3% pooled); survival benefit not proven.
Conversion does not open transplantation (iCCA-B4).
questions.why: The conversion evidence comes mostly from locally advanced disease. For metastatic iCCA it rests on very small, selected series, and unselected metastatic resection gives poor survival.

evidence.design_population: Meta-analysis and pooled patient data, 466 patients (49.6% iCCA).
evidence.selection: Of 55 iCCA, 19 had metastatic disease before conversion, mostly nodal; most series are locally advanced only.
evidence.results: Conversion associated with longer survival than non-surgical care (HR 0.39); metastatic presentation worse on univariable but not multivariable analysis; residual nodal metastasis in the specimen HR 14.7 (2.3–93.9).

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 101 unresectable biliary cancers; 20 converted.
evidence.selection: 14 converted had distant disease (liver 6, para-aortic nodes 5, peritoneal 3).
evidence.results: 5-year survival 55.0% with conversion vs 8.6% without, from the start of chemotherapy; recurrence 14 of 20.
evidence.limits: Mixed biliary subsites; immortal-time bias; not iCCA-specific; the abstract gives 65.0% vs 4.3%, inconsistent with the text.

evidence.selection: No response or metastatic-site data.
evidence.results: 3-year survival 13.8% with surgery vs 3% without.

evidence.selection: Locally advanced, not metastatic.
evidence.results: 39 (53%) resected after chemotherapy, median survival 24.1 months (similar to upfront resection).
evidence.locator: Br J Surg 2017 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Resection with lymphadenectomy; timing relative to chemotherapy not stated in the abstract.
evidence.results: Nodes beyond the hepatoduodenal, common hepatic artery and peripancreatic area: median survival 13.3 vs 24.3 months (p=0.047).

evidence.selection: Locally advanced.
evidence.results: Clavien–Dindo ≥III 60.7%; postoperative mortality 8.9%; 5-year survival 39.1%.
evidence.locator: J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2024 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: No distant disease.
evidence.results: 24 (10.9%) resected after systemic therapy; median survival 22.5 vs 19.9 months.
evidence.locator: Int J Cancer 2026 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Guidelines are characterized as discouraging surgery for metastatic iCCA; benefit in metastatic disease is unproven.
questions.certainty: Low for regional nodal disease after response; very low for distant disease.
questions.change: Prospective data on conversion surgery for metastatic iCCA.

questions.title: Previously malignant nodes, peritoneal or distant disease
questions.question: Should regional nodal disease that has responded, or any treated peritoneal or distant disease, ever allow transplantation for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.position: Keep closed. Nodal, peritoneal or distant disease found at any time, including at operative staging and after response to chemoradiation or chemotherapy, ends the transplant route; there is no re-entry after nodal response. The data on transplantation after nodal disease are absent rather than negative, and that is recorded.
rules: Before neoadjuvant chemoradiation: EUS-FNA of any suspicious regional node (not through the primary). A positive node ends the route.
Operative staging before transplantation with biopsy of hepatic artery and pericholedochal nodes and of any suspicious lesion.
Previously proven malignant nodes stay excluded even after radiographic or pathological clearance; distant or peritoneal disease at any time ends the route.
questions.why: Nodal disease is the commonest finding that removes patients at staging, and survival after removal is short. One US centre accepted regional N1 disease and four patients were transplanted with metastases, without separable outcomes, so there are no usable data either way.

evidence.selection: Staging findings overlap: positive nodes 19, peritoneal 14, local extension 11.
evidence.results: Median survival after the staging operation 6.0 months; EUS-FNA before chemoradiation lowered the positive-staging rate to 15%; two node-positive patients (one also with omental metastases) lived 3.7 and 8.7 years without transplant.

evidence.selection: Positive staging biopsies excluded patients in most centres; one centre accepted N0–N1 within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
evidence.results: Staging found metastases in 17%; 4 transplanted with metastatic disease, pooled in a 48-patient outside-criteria group (recurrence HR 2.98); explant nodal invasion 14% with recurrence vs 4% without.
evidence.limits: Centre-dependent handling; no separate estimate for nodal disease.

evidence.selection: Imaging suspicion pooled with tissue proof.
evidence.results: Of 498 fit unresected patients, 156 had nodal and 179 distant metastases; only 34 (5%) potentially eligible.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2020; Results, Fig. 1, Table 3.

evidence.selection: EUS or laparoscopic FNA of suspicious regional nodes; patients with metastases excluded; operative biopsy of hepatic artery and pericholedochal nodes.
evidence.results: No outcome data.

evidence.selection: Explant nodes.
evidence.results: Node positivity predicted recurrence (HR 3.27), not survival; not significant in the intentional pCCA/iCCA subset (HR 2.48).

evidence.selection: Any malignant node precludes further screening.
evidence.results: EUS sampling found malignant nodes in 3 of 75; surgical staging found non-regional malignant nodes in 6 of 43.

evidence.design_population: Prospective pilot, 18 hilar and intrahepatic tumors.
evidence.selection: Admitted regional lymphadenopathy without distant metastasis; nodal pathology not reported in the abstract.
evidence.results: 5 transplanted; one isolated portacaval nodal recurrence at 12 months.

questions.counter: Absence of usable data is not proof of futility; a small regional-node subset may do well.
questions.certainty: Moderate that conventional selection gives better outcomes; very low or none for a cleared-node pathway.
questions.change: A prospective series transplanting tissue-proven regional N1 disease after response, with intention-to-treat survival.

questions.title: Resection after nodal or distant disease responds
questions.question: When perihilar cholangiocarcinoma has regional, para-aortic or distant disease that responds, when is resection reasonable?
questions.position: Regional nodal disease goes to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and then resection in responders, recognizing that a survival benefit is not established. Para-aortic or other non-regional nodes are not resected upfront; after durable response with negative re-sampling, MDT case-by-case only. Distant metastasis stays systemic-therapy-led; conversion only exceptionally. Any nodal disease still excludes transplantation (pCCA-B1).
rules: Regional nodes: FDG-PET-positive or tissue-proven regional nodes → neoadjuvant chemotherapy, restaging, resection if no distant disease.
Para-aortic nodes: upfront data conflict; do not resect when known. After response, consider only with negative intraoperative sampling.
Distant metastasis: systemic therapy (gemcitabine–cisplatin-based); conversion only within a registry.
questions.why: Upfront series disagree on para-aortic nodes, and no pCCA-specific post-response series exists (only 5 mixed-subsite para-aortic cases). Japanese conversion data are mixed biliary cancers.

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 110 pCCA; 72 received neoadjuvant gemcitabine–S-1.
evidence.selection: Regional nodes defined by FDG-PET uptake only; distant disease excluded.
evidence.results: Curative resection 85.1%, 65.8% and 24.0% in resectable, borderline and locally advanced groups.
evidence.limits: No survival for node-positive patients; benefit not established.

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 20 conversions of biliary cancer.
evidence.selection: 5 with para-aortic nodes; all 5 were negative on para-aortic sampling at conversion resection (in 3 the nodes had disappeared on imaging).
evidence.results: One pCCA patient (para-aortic nodes cleared) had axial nodal recurrence 11 months after conversion.

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 143 with intraoperative para-aortic sampling.
evidence.selection: Upfront surgery.
evidence.results: Para-aortic metastasis in 17 (11.9%); PET identified only 17.6%; with para-aortic metastasis, survival did not differ with or without resection (15.6 vs 18.0 months, p=0.790).
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2026 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: 16 with para-aortic metastasis resected.
evidence.results: Median survival 33.7 vs 16.7 months (resected vs unresected); not worse than regional node-positive.
evidence.limits: Very small; perihilar and distal mixed.
evidence.locator: World J Surg 2020 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Para-aortic data conflict; post-response evidence is limited to a handful of mixed-subsite cases.
questions.certainty: Low for regional nodes after response; very low for non-regional or distant disease.
questions.change: A post-response series of resection with para-aortic or distant disease.

questions.title: Previously treated extrahepatic disease
questions.question: Should a lung-only study stratum be opened for completely treated pulmonary metastases, and if so with which interval and biology limits? All other previously treated extrahepatic sites stay closed.
questions.position: Keep previously treated extrahepatic disease closed in the CRLM transplant pathway. IHPBA Statement 9 finds no evidence to support transplantation for patients who initially present with or later develop extrahepatic metastases, and TransMet excluded previous or concomitant extrahepatic disease. Propose one narrow study stratum (not active) for limited, completely treated lung-only metastases; every other site stays closed.
rules: Default: extrahepatic metastasis after primary resection (including nodes outside the primary field), metastasis removed with the primary, and local relapse are outside the pathway, even after resection, ablation, radiotherapy or complete response. Response to systemic therapy alone never counts as clearance.

Proposed lung-only study stratum (needs its own protocol, IRB and a living-donor or individually reviewed allocation route): at most three lung metastases, each completely treated with curative intent, no thoracic nodal involvement, and no recurrence for ≥12 months after the last lung treatment (SECA-III excludes resection of lung or hilar-node metastases within the last year and of other non-hepatic metastases within 2 years; the Japanese protocol uses >6 months recurrence-free). The meeting must choose the interval.
The stratum adds no other relaxation: every CRLM-B3 limit applies, and favorable biology is required (low Oslo or Fong score; low liver metabolic tumor volume). Chest CT and PET-CT within one month.
Hilar nodes: frozen section of hilar nodes before implantation, and before donor hepatectomy in living donation. A positive node ends the transplant.

Closed with no stratum: nodal disease outside the primary field; peritoneal, ovarian, adrenal, bone, brain or other non-lung sites; local relapse; more than three lung lesions; thoracic nodes; recurrence after lung treatment.
questions.why: Lung-limited disease is the most indolent extrahepatic pattern, and post-transplant lung recurrence is often resectable, but outcome data for transplantation after treated extrahepatic disease are limited to two SECA-II recipients (a lung metastasis resected 8 years earlier, recurrence-free; an ovarian metastasis removed 14 months earlier, lung relapse at 5 months). In the Oslo series, hilar node metastasis on frozen section at laparotomy was the commonest extrahepatic reason for not transplanting (7 of 10).

evidence.selection: Excluded “previous or concomitant extrahepatic metastases or local recurrence” (Methods); every transplant preceded by exploration with frozen section of suspicious nodes.
evidence.results: 5-year survival 56.6% vs 12.6% (HR 0.37); recurrence mainly in the lung, with curative-intent salvage in 12 of 26.
evidence.limits: Benefit cannot be transferred to previously treated extrahepatic disease.

evidence.selection: Statement 9: no evidence supports transplantation for patients who initially present with or subsequently develop extrahepatic metastases; node-positive patients excluded; no lung exception or nodule-size rule.
evidence.results: Statement 41: isolated pulmonary recurrence after transplantation should be considered for resection.

evidence.selection: Protocol allowed resectable lung lesions <15 mm and prior nodal or local relapse treated >1 year earlier.
evidence.results: Only 1 recipient had a previously resected lung metastasis (8 years earlier) and was recurrence-free; a second had an ovarian metastasis removed with the primary 14 months earlier and relapsed in the lung at 5 months; the arm’s median survival of 18 months reflects other high-risk features.
evidence.limits: Protocol precedent only, not outcome evidence about lung disease.

evidence.selection: PET-CT before transplant; prior extrahepatic disease not analysed.
evidence.results: 10 of 72 not transplanted for extrahepatic disease, 7 with hilar node metastasis on frozen section at laparotomy; intention-to-treat 5-year survival 42.6%.

evidence.selection: Liver-confined disease.
evidence.results: 1 of 10 had PET-negative portal nodal metastasis and recurred in the peritoneum at 121 days.

evidence.selection: Liver-only disease required.
evidence.results: On retrospective review, 7 had untreated lung metastases already present at transplant; no statistical test reported.
evidence.limits: Not evidence that treated lung disease is safe.

evidence.design_population: Oslo, 14 recipients with resected lung relapse after transplant.
evidence.selection: Post-transplant setting.
evidence.results: 10-year survival 64.5% from first lung resection; 85.7% with liver metabolic tumor volume <70 cm³ vs 25.0% above.
evidence.limits: Selected patients; does not address pre-transplant disease.

evidence.selection: Admits ≤3 lung metastases without recurrence for >6 months after treatment; no size limit.
evidence.results: Protocol only.

evidence.selection: Resectable lung lesions <15 mm allowed. Excluded: resection of lung or hilar-node metastases within 1 year, of local relapse or other non-hepatic metastasis within 2 years, and any previous bone, CNS or thoracic or abdominal nodal metastasis.
evidence.results: Recruiting.

evidence.design_population: Randomized trial of lung metastasectomy, 93 patients (29% after liver resection).
evidence.selection: No other sites than treated liver metastases.
evidence.results: Adjusted HR 0.87 (0.51–1.48); 5-year survival 29.6% without metastasectomy vs 36.4% with.

evidence.selection: Lung metastases after transplant.
evidence.results: Median doubling time 125 vs 130 days (transplant vs controls).
evidence.locator: Br J Surg 2018 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: The lung-only signal comes from post-transplant relapse and protocol precedent, not from transplantation after treated lung disease. PulMiCC was inconclusive but found 29.6% 5-year survival without metastasectomy, suggesting that lung metastasectomy may select favorable biology rather than cure it.
questions.certainty: Very low for transplantation after previously treated extrahepatic disease; low for the indirect inference that lung-limited disease behaves indolently after transplant.
questions.change: SECA-III or Japanese protocol results in recipients with treated lung metastases.

questions.title: Liver resection when extrahepatic disease is treated or treatable
questions.question: When colorectal cancer has extrahepatic disease that is treated or completely treatable, when should liver resection be offered?
questions.position: Treated or completely treatable extrahepatic disease is not an absolute contraindication to curative-intent liver resection, but complete clearance of every site is mandatory and benefit depends on the site. Lung disease has the best outcome; nodal disease does poorly (pooled 5-year survival about 15%), worst beyond the hepatic pedicle; limited peritoneal disease belongs to expert CRS/HIPEC centres. Any extrahepatic disease ends transplant intent (CRLM-B5).
rules: Lung: combined or staged liver and lung metastasectomy after joint HPB–thoracic review when every lesion can be removed; a prior lung resection does not exclude liver resection.

Portal (hepatoduodenal) nodes: resect only with complete lymphadenectomy after response to chemotherapy, with explicit counselling; coeliac, para-aortic and retroperitoneal nodes generally not. Portal and retroperitoneal nodes did equally poorly in the largest single-institution series (MSKCC); a Paris series found pedicular nodes better than coeliac or para-aortic nodes (5-year survival 25% vs 0%).
Peritoneum: limited peritoneal disease with liver metastases only in a peritoneal-surface-malignancy centre (CRS/HIPEC plus limited liver resection).
Counsel: recurrence about 90%; 10-year disease-free survival about 3% after resection with extrahepatic disease.
questions.why: Pooled and registry data show useful survival after complete resection of lung disease and poorer survival with nodal or peritoneal disease; the only randomized trial of lung metastasectomy was inconclusive.

evidence.design_population: Meta-analysis, 52 studies, 15,144 patients (2,308 with extrahepatic disease).
evidence.selection: Synchronous or previous extrahepatic disease resected with the liver.
evidence.results: 5-year survival: lung 26% (15–39%), peritoneum 17%, nodes 15%; R0 at both sites lowered the risk of death (RR 0.73).

evidence.design_population: MSKCC, 219 hepatectomies with resected extrahepatic disease.
evidence.selection: Synchronous disease, resected within 6 months.
evidence.results: Portal vs retroperitoneal nodes: no survival difference (p=0.768); incomplete extrahepatic resection: no survivors beyond 3.5 years; disease-free at 10 years 3.2%.

evidence.selection: Lung metastases after colorectal resection.
evidence.results: Adjusted HR 0.87 (0.51–1.48); inconclusive.

evidence.design_population: Cancer Care Ontario guideline (archived December 2020; evidence to January 2010).
evidence.selection: Liver and lung metastases.
evidence.results: Combined or staged metastasectomy recommended when all lung metastases can be removed; liver resection may follow a prior lung resection; routine liver resection not recommended with portal nodal disease.

evidence.selection: 149 liver plus lung resections vs 9,185 liver-only.
evidence.results: Adjusted 5-year survival 44.5% vs 51.5%; 14.3% when lung disease was not resected.
evidence.locator: Br J Surg 2015 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Nodes after chemotherapy.
evidence.results: 5-year survival 25% pedicular vs 0% coeliac or para-aortic.
evidence.locator: J Clin Oncol 2008 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Synchronous peritoneal and liver metastases.
evidence.results: CRS/HIPEC with liver treatment: 5-year survival 37%.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2025 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Peritoneal disease with vs without liver metastases.
evidence.results: Overall survival HR 1.68 with liver metastases.
evidence.locator: Int J Hyperthermia 2020 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Benefit is not proven by randomization; lung metastasectomy itself was inconclusive in PulMiCC.
questions.change: Randomized data on metastasectomy in combined liver and lung disease.

questions.title: Previously treated extrahepatic disease
questions.question: Which previously treated extrahepatic NET sites may enter the transplant route: resected regional nodes only, or also distant nodes and a solitary treated bone lesion as ENETS 2026 suggests?
questions.status: Resected regional nodes only, after clearance
questions.position: Previously resected regional nodal disease is already within Milan-NET when the primary and all extrahepatic deposits were removed in a separate curative operation and restaging at least 6 months later shows no disease. Previously resected distant nodes need individual review. Previous lung, bone or other solid-organ metastasis stays closed, including after complete treatment; ENETS 2026 would accept a solitary locally treated bone lesion as expert opinion, recorded as a disagreement.
rules: Regional (mesenteric, peripancreatic) nodes resected with the primary in a separate operation: eligible after ≥6 months without recurrence and negative SSTR-PET with CT/MRI within 3 months of transplant consideration.
Distant nodes previously resected, or nodal disease cleared only by PRRT, ablation or radiotherapy: individual review only, with SSTR-PET-negative status for ≥6 months.
Lung, bone (including a solitary treated lesion), peritoneal or other organ metastasis: closed. Spinal or brain metastases and unresectable mesenteric root disease: closed in every framework.
Stage the primary and any major organ resection before transplantation, not at it. Plan hilar lymphadenectomy; counsel that nodal involvement on final pathology is associated with worse survival.
questions.why: Milan-NET itself requires all extrahepatic deposits removed before transplant consideration, and 81% of the Milan recipients had resected node-positive primaries. No series in this evidence set reports outcomes after previously treated distant disease; the registry series did not record pre-transplant extrahepatic status. Bone metastases are independently adverse and rarely cleared.

evidence.selection: Milan-NET: primary removed “with all extrahepatic deposits in a separate curative resection prior to transplant consideration”; restaging 6 months after removal.
evidence.results: 81% of recipients had node-positive primaries and 57% hilar node-positive; 5- and 10-year survival 97.2% and 88.8%.
evidence.limits: Non-randomized; no outcome split by nodal status.

evidence.selection: Exclusion of extrahepatic disease; hilar lymphadenectomy at transplant.
evidence.results: Nodal involvement on final pathology: survival HR 5.7 (1.3–24), univariate; after transplantation, first recurrences most often involved distant nodes (16 of 25, 64%) and bone (9 of 25, 36%).

evidence.selection: Replace “no extrahepatic disease” with “no macroscopic, non-targetable” disease; examples: isolated resectable nodes or a solitary bone lesion amenable to local treatment.
evidence.results: Excludes unresectable mesenteric nodes, spinal and brain metastases; sets no interval after extrahepatic treatment.

evidence.design_population: Two Swedish centres, 138 with bone metastases.
evidence.selection: Bone metastases on SSTR-PET; rarely biopsied; never curatively treated.
evidence.results: Any bone metastasis HR 1.94; 21% with ≤5 lesions progressed to >5.

evidence.selection: Concurrent surgery at transplant (84 patients) included extended lymphadenectomy (38), primary resection (29), organ resections and peritonectomy.
evidence.results: Major concurrent resection HR 3.1 (all eras); after 2000, any concurrent resection HR 1.9 (p=0.058).

evidence.design_population: 28 centres (mostly US, also Canadian and European), 85 transplants.
evidence.selection: “Extent of resection” = concurrent primary or multivisceral surgery, not metastasis clearance.
evidence.results: Extensive concurrent surgery associated with worse survival (p=0.015).

evidence.selection: Transplant candidates.
evidence.results: PET removed 7 of 15 candidates.

questions.counter: ENETS 2026 and some series suggest limited bone disease may not worsen survival; the bone exclusion is a conservative local choice.
questions.certainty: Low for resected regional nodes after a recurrence-free interval; very low for distant nodes, PRRT-only clearance and solid-organ metastases.
questions.change: Transplant outcomes in recipients with previously treated distant or bone disease.

questions.title: Liver surgery when extrahepatic disease is present or treated
questions.question: Does present or previously treated extrahepatic disease preclude liver cytoreduction or resection for well-differentiated NET liver metastases?
questions.position: Extrahepatic disease does not by itself preclude hepatic cytoreduction or resection of the primary for well-differentiated G1–G2 disease when at least 70% of liver disease can be removed or treated and accessible extrahepatic disease can be resected at the same time. Frame it as life-prolonging debulking; extrahepatic disease is associated with shorter survival in most, but not all, series (NANETS describes the data as conflicting).
rules: Proceed when ≥70% debulking is achievable and accessible extrahepatic disease (mesenteric nodes, limited peritoneal deposits) can be removed; resect distant nodes only when this renders the patient free of visible disease.
Bone metastases are an adverse modifier, not an automatic exclusion; diffuse skeletal, brain or unresectable mesenteric-root disease argue against surgery.
No observation period is required before cytoreduction.
Transplant questions go to NET-B4.
questions.why: NANETS consensus accepts extrahepatic disease for cytoreduction; cohorts show it shortens survival.

evidence.selection: Recommendation 5d: extrahepatic disease is not an absolute contraindication to cytoreduction; 5c: patients with extrahepatic disease may be eligible for liver debulking when ≥70% debulking is achievable.
evidence.results: Distant nodes resected only in select cases (threatening vital structures, or to achieve no evidence of disease).

evidence.selection: Extrahepatic distant metastases in 16% (peritoneum, bone).
evidence.results: Associated with worse overall survival, not progression-free survival; median survival 122 months overall.

evidence.selection: Nodes not counted as extrahepatic.
evidence.results: Liver resection (n=23): 5-year survival 78%; non-surgical liver-directed therapy median survival 13 vs 16 months with none (not formally compared; the authors read liver-directed therapy favourably).

evidence.selection: On SSTR-PET.
evidence.results: Any bone metastasis HR 1.94; >5 lesions median survival 18 vs 75 months.

evidence.selection: Resection.
evidence.results: Extrahepatic metastasis HR 3.9 for death.
evidence.limits: Not split by treated vs untreated.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2018 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Recurrence sites.
evidence.results: 10-year survival 0% with extrahepatic-only recurrence.
evidence.locator: J Surg Oncol 2017 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 55 cytoreductions with extrahepatic disease.
evidence.selection: 87% combined intra- and extrahepatic.
evidence.results: Major morbidity 18%, mortality 3.6%.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2018 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: All evidence is observational and selected.

questions.title: Primary resection or cytoreduction with extrahepatic disease
questions.question: With pancreatic NET metastases outside the liver, should the primary be removed or the liver cytoreduced?
questions.position: Extrahepatic disease should not by itself contraindicate primary resection or hepatic cytoreduction (NANETS 2020), but the decision rests on local complications, symptoms and response to other therapy, and extrahepatic disease tempers the expected durability. Surgery here is palliative debulking, not curative-intent resection.
rules: Favor surgery for symptomatic or functional tumors, body–tail primaries and G1–G2 disease when debulking is substantial.
Transplantation for pancreatic NET metastases follows NET-B4 (portal-drained primary resected first).
questions.why: Primary resection is associated with lower mortality in pooled observational data that are strongly confounded; a recent series found no survival benefit.

evidence.selection: Extrahepatic disease “should not necessarily” contraindicate primary removal or cytoreduction; data limited and conflicting.
evidence.results: No transplant recommendation.

evidence.selection: Primary resection with unresectable liver metastases.
evidence.results: Lower risk of death (OR 0.38, 0.23–0.65).

evidence.design_population: Single centre, 118 with synchronous liver metastases.
evidence.selection: Asymptomatic pNET.
evidence.results: Primary resection did not change survival (median 10 years); extrahepatic disease predicted progression.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2025 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.title: Extrahepatic disease (EHD component)
questions.question: Should a lung-only extrahepatic stratum be activated for hepatic EHE, given the conflict between the 2021 consensus (no transplantation with extrahepatic disease) and the registry data?
questions.position: Start with liver-only disease and no macrovascular invasion. Keep the lung-only stratum defined but not activated: limited lung disease that is stable through an observation period or completely resected. Nodal (beyond hilar), pleural or other serosal, bone, peritoneal, progressive or symptomatic disease stays closed. The explant-based HEHE-LT score is for post-transplant surveillance, not selection.
rules: Lung-only stratum (not active): asymptomatic, no pleural involvement, stable on serial imaging for ≥6 months or completely resected or ablated with no recurrence for ≥6 months; independent expert review and a written comparison with observation or systemic therapy.
A waiting time longer than 120 days is a usable pre-transplant test of time; shorter waits were associated with recurrence.
Hilar nodal involvement is a recurrence risk factor, not an extrahepatic exclusion; plan hilar lymphadenectomy. Nodes beyond the hilum are extrahepatic disease and are closed.
Record the guideline–registry disagreement in every case.
questions.why: The registry finding that extrahepatic disease was not adverse is an absence of evidence: it was mostly untreated lung disease and the hazard ratio was 1.5 with a wide interval. The consensus exclusion is expert opinion.

evidence.selection: Pre-transplant extrahepatic disease on imaging in 40 (lung 23, nodes 8); only 5 had lung surgery beforehand.
evidence.results: Extrahepatic disease HR 1.5 (0.8–3.0), not retained; hilar nodes HR 2.2; waiting ≤120 days HR 2.5; the HEHE-LT score uses explant pathology.
evidence.limits: Absence of evidence, not equivalence; registry without dropouts.

evidence.selection: Transplantation “should not be proposed” with extrahepatic disease [V, A].
evidence.results: Level V evidence (expert opinion) with grade A strength.

evidence.selection: Nodal and pleural disease recorded.
evidence.results: Nodal involvement HR 2.7; 5-year survival 30% with nodal and 22% with pleural disease.

evidence.selection: Extrahepatic disease on imaging in 49%, mostly lung; most patients had non-surgical, largely systemic therapy, and local treatment of extrahepatic sites is not reported.
evidence.results: Extrahepatic disease not prognostic on univariable analysis of the whole cohort, 96% managed without transplant (HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.64–2.73); 8 transplants, confounded.

evidence.selection: 10 had extrahepatic disease before or at transplant.
evidence.results: 1-, 5- and 10-year survival 90%, 80% and 80% with vs 94%, 83% and 70% without.

evidence.selection: Extrahepatic metastases in 26 at diagnosis.
evidence.results: Bone metastasis HR 6.3; lung not adverse (HR 0.8).
evidence.locator: J Surg Oncol 2024 (abstract; full text pending).

questions.counter: Registry survival with pre-transplant extrahepatic disease (mostly lung) is good, so a blanket bar may be too strict.
questions.certainty: Low for prognostic association; very low for benefit of transplantation with extrahepatic disease.
questions.change: Prospective outcomes of transplantation with limited lung disease after observation.

questions.title: Surgery after oligometastatic disease responds
questions.question: When synchronous oligometastatic PDAC responds to chemotherapy, or isolated lung metastases appear late, should surgery be offered outside a trial?
questions.position: Distant metastasis stays systemic-therapy-led. Response-selected conversion surgery for limited liver metastases is offered preferably within a trial (METAPANC, CSPAC-1) or a registry after MDT review. Metachronous isolated lung metastases after a long disease-free interval may be resected. There is no PDAC transplant pathway.
rules: Synchronous liver oligometastases: ≤3 liver metastases (OligoPanc working definition, relative-majority only; METAPANC ≤3 liver-only), no peritoneal or other extrahepatic disease, induction chemotherapy without progression (METAPANC: 8 cycles of mFOLFIRINOX; Heidelberg: usually ≥6 cycles with RECIST response of metastases and a marker fall), CA19-9 fall >50% to <500 U/mL (CSPAC-1), resectable primary and metastases.

Counsel: in Heidelberg, 46% were unresectable at exploration and only about 1 in 4 explored was ypM0; median survival 25.5 months (ypM0) vs 10.7 (ypM1) vs 8.1 (exploration only). Surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis did worse.
Metachronous isolated lung metastases: ≤3 (ideally solitary), unilateral, disease-free interval of about 2 years (17–28 months cited), after systemic therapy and MDT review.

Para-aortic (16b1) nodes known before surgery are systemic disease and outside the OligoPanc Delphi definition (although panellists rated a para-aortic nodal vignette as oligometastatic); when found at operation, do not abort resection on 16b1 alone.
questions.why: Survival after resection is concentrated in complete responders, and unselected resection of metastases does not help. Trial rules give the clearest selection thresholds.

evidence.design_population: Heidelberg, 173 explored after chemotherapy for metastatic PDAC.
evidence.selection: RECIST PR/CR of metastases plus a fall in CA19-9 and CEA, usually ≥6 cycles.
evidence.results: 93 resected (45 ypM0); median survival 25.5 vs 10.7 vs 8.1 months; CA19-9 ≥400 HR 2.31; surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis HR 1.82.
evidence.limits: Single referral centre; no intention-to-treat denominator.

evidence.selection: ≤3 lesions in one organ (liver or lung) reached only relative majority (58% and 42%); systemic therapy before local treatment in synchronous disease (82%).
evidence.results: No induction duration or response thresholds defined.

evidence.selection: ≤3 liver metastases, no extrahepatic disease; 8 cycles mFOLFIRINOX; CR, PR or stable disease randomized.
evidence.results: No results yet.

evidence.selection: ≤3 liver foci; randomization requires SD/PR and CA19-9 fall >50% to <500 U/mL.
evidence.results: No results located.

evidence.selection: Only 42% had chemotherapy before surgery; response rarely reported and not analysed.
evidence.results: Surgery associated with longer survival (HR 0.41); the HR 0.18 figure is a model scenario, not an observed effect.
evidence.limits: Retrospective; misattributed coefficient in the abstract.

evidence.design_population: Meta-analysis, 9 studies, 467 patients with lung metastases.
evidence.selection: Mostly metachronous after pancreatectomy; chemotherapy before lung resection uncommon.
evidence.results: Pooled HR 0.637 (0.531–0.764); significant publication bias; survival from pancreatectomy.

evidence.selection: Lung metastases.
evidence.results: Metastasectomy 33.0 vs 19.0 months (n=24, unadjusted).

evidence.selection: Station 16b1 sampled at upfront surgery.
evidence.results: PDAC 16b1-positive median survival 10 vs 24 months (aHR 2.33); authors advise against aborting resection on 16b1 alone.

evidence.selection: Preoperative therapy and response selection not described in the abstract.
evidence.results: 5-year survival 8.1% (liver) and 10.1% (interaortocaval nodes).
evidence.locator: Eur J Surg Oncol 2016 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.design_population: Johns Hopkins, 22 synchronous hepatic resections (17 pancreatic, 5 other periampullary).
evidence.selection: Simultaneous with resection of the primary; preoperative therapy not stated in the abstract.
evidence.results: Median survival 5.9 vs 5.6 months with bypass alone.

evidence.selection: Disappearance of liver metastases and CA19-9 fall.
evidence.results: R0 88%; complete pathological response 17%.
evidence.locator: Ann Surg Oncol 2017 (abstract; full text pending).

evidence.selection: Median 10.4 months of chemotherapy.
evidence.results: Survival after conversion 39.7 months.

questions.counter: Guidelines do not primarily recommend surgery for hepatic oligometastases; randomized results are pending.
questions.certainty: Low for response-selected liver oligometastases; low for late isolated lung metastases; very low for distant nodes.

questions.title: Local treatment after metastatic disease responds
questions.question: When metastatic ampullary adenocarcinoma responds to systemic therapy, should limited liver or lung metastases be treated locally?
questions.position: Systemic therapy is the default for metastatic ampullary adenocarcinoma. Local therapy or surgery for limited liver or lung metastases that respond durably is a case-by-case MDT decision, extrapolated from PDAC and biliary data; there is no ampullary-specific evidence after response.
rules: Apply the PDAC-R1 selection rules by analogy (limited sites, no progression, marker fall, complete resectability).
Isolated late lung recurrence has a better prognosis than synchronous or liver metastases.
Station 16b1 involvement found at upfront surgery is prognostically poor but is not by itself a reason to abort resection.
questions.why: The only registry analysis measured resection of the primary, not metastasectomy after response.

evidence.selection: Primary-tumor resection; no metastatic-site or response data.
evidence.results: Matched median survival 16 vs 8 months; association strongest without chemotherapy (selection).

evidence.selection: Upfront surgery; adjuvant therapy in 4%.
evidence.results: 16b1-positive (n=7): median survival 9 vs 62 months (aHR 4.35).

evidence.selection: Metastasectomy of pancreatic and periampullary cancer.
evidence.results: Ampullary primaries and isolated pulmonary recurrence had better prognosis.

evidence.selection: Systemic therapy in all stages.
evidence.results: “Select tumors may be treated surgically.”

questions.counter: Evidence cannot distinguish surgery from systemic therapy alone.
questions.change: Any ampullary series of surgery after response.

not_applicable.position: Not applicable. HCA is benign; extrahepatic disease arises only after malignant transformation (about 3–4% in pooled series, 3.1% series-only), when the HCC route and HCC-B5 apply. The HCA pathway already requires no extrahepatic metastasis and no macrovascular invasion where transformation is confirmed.
Not applicable. Cystic lesions are premalignant; an invasive carcinoma with metastases is managed on the PDAC roadmap (PDAC-R1).

Different question. A previously treated extrahepatic cancer is already a risk factor in this roadmap: an indeterminate liver lesion in such a patient is worked up with MRI as a possible metastasis and routed to the matching tumor pathway.
